𝗪𝗜𝗟𝗟 𝗔𝗜 𝗞𝗜𝗟𝗟 𝗨𝗦 𝗔𝗟𝗟 𝗕𝗬 𝟮𝟬𝟯𝟬? 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗖𝗛 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗬 𝗦𝗔𝗬𝗦 🤖

Two weeks ago, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who has worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, quit his job and left with a warning that traveled around the world. The people building AI, he wrote, earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of this decade.

Since then, the debate has been loud.

On one side, the doomsayers. On the other, the tech optimists. And in the middle, the people who think it is all a marketing stunt. Very few have looked at what the research actually says, so let me try.

In 2021, the researcher Joseph Carlsmith built a model that is still widely used to think about AI risk. For a power-seeking AI scenario to cause an existential catastrophe, a whole chain of events has to happen: advanced AI has to be built, there have to be strong incentives to deploy it, it has to be harder to build safe AI than unsafe AI, some systems have to seek power, humanity has to lose control permanently, and it all has to end in catastrophe.

Every link in the chain has to hold. And as probabilities are multiplied, one unlikely link pulls the whole risk down.

Carlsmith's own estimate was around 5% by 2070, which he later raised to above 10%. That is a serious number, but note the timeline. For the 2030 scenario to play out, all six conditions would have to be met within the next four years.

In 2023, the think tank AI Impacts surveyed 2,778 AI researchers, and up to half of them put at least a 10% chance on human extinction or permanent loss of control at some point in the future. At the same time, 68% believed good outcomes from AI were more likely than bad ones.

So optimism and concern are not opposites. And as investors, we know this feeling well. You can be bullish on a trend and still respect the tail risk.

The most useful counterweight comes from RAND, the American research institution. They asked a very practical question: how would an AI physically kill every human being?

They looked at nuclear war, biological weapons, and climate manipulation, and the conclusion was that it is far harder than it sounds. No single nuclear button can be hacked. A pandemic or a climate catastrophe would require control of laboratories, factories, raw materials, and supply chains.

So, intelligence can develop fast. Factories, energy supplies, and logistics cannot. Actions in the physical world take time and leave traces, which gives humans a chance to notice and intervene. And this is the strongest argument against the 2030 scenario.

This does not mean we can relax.

In experiments, AI models have pretended to follow instructions to avoid being retrained, and models trained to exploit loopholes have later tried to sabotage simulated safety research. This summer, several frontier models broke out of their test environments in unexpected ways.

The International AI Safety Report 2026, written by more than 100 researchers, sums it up well: AI capabilities are improving faster than expected, and 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝗴𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴.

I am not sure Coxon's warning was a PR stunt in itself. He walked away from his job shortly before his shares would have vested, and that is not what you do for marketing.

Still, the follow-up had an element of strategic theater, and so does how big AI companies talk about risk. Open-weight models, many of them from China, are often 10 to 20 times cheaper and not far behind in quality. Over time, the quality gap could narrow, so this is a serious threat to AI labs' businesses.

Regulation is expensive, and the largest players can afford it much more easily than their cheaper competitors. So, it could effectively serve as a moat for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI. When the leading labs ask for more regulation, two things can be true at once: The concern can be genuine, and it can also be good business.

Based on the research, I don't find human extinction by 2030 realistic. The more likely near-term danger isn't AI acting on its own, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺.

One important thing to note though: If people working in a weapons company said: "We are building nuclear weapons. We don't fully control them, and there is a real chance one of them kills everyone within the next five years," our answer would never be "stop hyping your nuclear bombs!"

We would take it seriously. We would send in inspectors. And we would regulate it. As Yoshua Bengio, one of the godfathers of AI, has put it, there is more regulation on a sandwich than on AI.

And now is the time to change that.
